summary: This note is a learning-psychology text on the mechanisms of learning, covering associative learning, classical conditioning (Pavlov), operant conditioning (Skinner), and observational learning (Bandura, mirror neurons). It explains key concepts such as acquisition, extinction, generalization, discrimination, reinforcement schedules, and shaping, and notes how cognitive and biological constraints limit conditioning. The surrounding page text is mostly 'section under development' boilerplate and was ignored; the note is cut off during the Bobo doll experiment.
one_line: Overview of learning mechanisms: classical and operant conditioning, observational learning, Pavlov, Skinner, Bandura and mirror neurons.
key_facts: Learning is defined in the note as a relatively permanent change in an organism's behavior due to experience.
In classical conditioning, acquisition occurs most readily when a CS is presented just before a US, ideally about a half-second before.
Pavlov received a medical degree at age 33 and his work on digestion earned him Russia's first Nobel prize in 1904.
Extinction is diminished responding that occurs when the CS no longer signals an impending US, as when Pavlov sounded the tone without presenting food.
Spontaneous recovery is the reappearance of a formerly extinguished response after a rest period, such as several hours in Pavlov's experiments.
Generalization is the tendency to respond to stimuli similar to a CS, while discrimination is the learned ability to distinguish a CS from other irrelevant stimuli.

Higher-order conditioning, also called second-order conditioning, lets a new neutral stimulus become a conditioned stimulus by association with a previously conditioned stimulus, though it tends to be weaker than first-stage conditioning.
Operant conditioning is the learning of associations between an organism's own behavior and its consequences; actions followed by reinforcers increase and actions followed by punishers decrease.
B. F. Skinner (1904–1990) built on Edward Thorndike's law of effect, stating that rewarded behavior is likely to recur, and used an operant chamber known as a Skinner box.
Shaping is a procedure in which reinforcers gradually guide an animal's actions toward a desired behavior through successive approximations.
Continuous reinforcement produces rapid learning but rapid extinction, while partial reinforcement produces slower initial learning but much greater resistance to extinction.

Fixed-ratio schedules reward after a set number of responses, variable-ratio after an unpredictable number, fixed-interval after set time periods, and variable-interval after unpredictable time periods.
Mirror neurons, located in the brain's frontal lobes, fire when a monkey performs an action or observes another doing so, providing a neural basis for imitation and observational learning.
Children see, children do: by age 14 months, children imitate acts modeled on TV, according to the note.
Albert Bandura is described as the pioneering researcher of observational learning, illustrated by the Bobo doll experiment in which a child watches an adult act aggressively toward an inflated doll.

entities.name: Ivan Pavlov
entities.role: Russian physiologist whose classic experiments on conditioning laid the foundation for behaviorism; studied digestion and won Russia's first Nobel prize in 1904

entities.name: John B. Watson
entities.role: Psychologist who built on Pavlov's work and named the position behaviorism, arguing psychology should study only overt behavior

entities.name: B. F. Skinner
entities.role: Psychologist (1904–1990) who expanded Thorndike's law of effect into operant conditioning and designed the Skinner box

entities.name: Edward L. Thorndike
entities.role: Psychologist who formulated the law of effect: rewarded behavior is likely to recur

entities.name: Albert Bandura
entities.role: Pioneering researcher of observational learning, known for the Bobo doll experiments

entities.name: Giacomo Rizzolatti
entities.role: Researcher who led the team that discovered mirror neurons in monkeys

entities.name: Andy Field
entities.role: Researcher who showed British children novel cartoon characters paired with ice cream or Brussels sprouts, so children came to like the ice-cream-associated characters best

entities.name: Michael Olson and Russell Fazio
entities.role: Researchers who classically conditioned adults' attitudes using little-known Pokémon characters

entities.name: Tirrell
entities.role: Individual who recounts experiencing extinction and spontaneous recovery after a breakup, with onion breath as the conditioned stimulus

entities.name: Skinner box
entities.role: Operant chamber designed by B. F. Skinner with a bar or key that animals press or peck to receive food or water, plus a device recording responses

entities.name: behaviorism
entities.role: The view that psychology should be an objective science studying behavior without reference to mental processes

entities.name: Russian Orthodox priesthood
entities.role: Career Pavlov initially planned to follow his father into before turning to medicine
